newsitem.title: ARGENTINA: Argentine Congress scraps "gag law" in ethics bill.
newsitem.headline: Argentine Congress scraps "gag law" in ethics bill.

text.p: Argentina's Congress on Wednesday scrapped controversial measures in a bill that could have jailed journalists for publishing public officials' sworn income statements.

The law envisaging two months to two years jail time for reporters using information for "malicious or hidden" ends was to be included in a public ethics bill for debate in the Chamber of Deputies, controlled by the ruling Peronists.
But members of the Chamber of Deputies' Constitutional Affairs Committee voted unanimously to scrap two articles that had been denounced as a Peronist attempt at a "gag law."
"Both articles have been eliminated unanimously," Deputy Jose Dumon of the opposition Radical Party told Reuters.
Debate on the public ethics bill was postponed.

President Carlos Menem's Peronist government has been embarrassed several times by corruption scandals involving senior public officials and a few months ago Interior Minister Carlos Corach, irritated by often critical media coverage, proposed the creation of a journalist ethics commission.
Peronist Congressman Carlos Soria had defended articles in the public ethics bill that he said would protect public officials from "fraudsters and kidnappers."

But opponents, vigorously supported by the news media, argued successfully that it was "in the public interest" for reporters to reveal information that could lead to the prosecution of corrupt officials.
